Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: For each support set $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ realized as $J=\operatorname{supp}q$ by some $q\in F$, define $C_J=\{v:\sum_i v_i=0,\ v_i\ge0\ (i\notin J),\ \langle v,w\rangle\le0\text{ for every }w\text{ with }\sum_iw_i=0,\ Mw=0,\ w_i\ge0\ (i\notin J)\}.$ This is a closed cone, being an intersection of closed linear constraints and closed half-spaces. If $v\in C_J$ and $Mv=0$, then $v$ is an allowed $w$ in its defining inequality, hence $\|v\|_2^2\le0$ and $v=0$.

Suppose $p\notin F$ and let $q$ be its nearest point in $F$, which is closed and convex. Put $J=\operatorname{supp}q$ and $v=(p-q)/\|p-q\|_2$. Then $\sum_i v_i=0$ and $v_i\ge0$ outside $J$, because $p_i\ge0=q_i$ there.

For each realized $J$, the set $C_J\cap\{v:\|v\|_2=1\}$ is compact by [F3]. If nonempty, the continuous function $v\mapsto\|Mv\|_2$ has a positive minimum $c_J$: a zero would contradict step 1.1. There are finitely many $J$, so the minimum $c$ of these positive $c_J$ is positive whenever any such unit section is nonempty. If all are empty, suppose $p\notin F$ and take its nearest point $q\in F$ by [F1]. With $J=\operatorname{supp}q$ and $v=(p-q)/\|p-q\|_2$, every vector $w$ in the tangent conditions defining $C_J$ has $q+tw\in F$ for small $t>0$. [F2] then gives $\langle v,w\rangle\le0$, so $v\in C_J$ and $\|v\|_2=1$, a contradiction. Hence $F=\Delta_d$ and the claim is immediate.

If $w$ satisfies the linear and sign conditions in the definition of $C_J$, then $q+tw\in F$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$: the affine equations are preserved, coordinates outside $J$ remain nonnegative, and the finitely many positive coordinates of $q$ on $J$ remain positive. By [F2], $\langle p-q,tw\rangle\le0$, so $\langle v,w\rangle\le0$ and $v\in C_J$.

For the nontrivial case of step 2.1, homogeneity and its constant $c$ give $\|Mp-b\|_2=\|M(p-q)\|_2=\|p-q\|_2\|Mv\|_2\ge c\operatorname{dist}_2(p,F)$. Taking $H=1/c$ proves the result for $p\notin F$; for $p\in F$ the left side is zero. In the empty-unit-section case from step 2.1, $F=\Delta_d$ and any $H>0$ works.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Divide each summand by $\sigma$, so it suffices to consider independent mean-zero variables with total variance one and $\beta:=\sum_i\mathbb E|X_i|^3$. A zero-variance summand is zero almost surely and may be removed. For $r>0$, let $\delta_m(r)$ be the supremum of the normal-CDF error over all $m$-term arrays with total variance one and third-moment sum at most $r^3$.

If some summand has variance greater than $1/2$, the needed Lyapunov inequality follows locally as follows. Put $A=|X_i|$ and $m_3=\mathbb EA^3$; then $m_3>0$. For $U=A/m_3^{1/3}$, the pointwise identity $1+2U^3-3U^2=(U-1)^2(2U+1)\ge0$ gives $\mathbb EA^2/m_3^{2/3}\le1$, so $\mathbb E|X_i|^3\ge(\mathbb EX_i^2)^{3/2}$. Therefore $\beta\ge(\mathbb EX_i^2)^{3/2}>1/(2\sqrt2)>1/3$. Since any two CDF values differ by at most one, the bound $\delta_m(r)\le1088r^3$ holds in this case.

It remains to prove the induction step when each summand variance is at most $1/2$. Fix a threshold $a$ and $\epsilon>0$, and let $h$ equal $1$ on $(-\infty,a]$, decrease linearly to $0$ on $[a,a+\epsilon]$, and equal $0$ afterward. Define $f(x)=e^{x^2/2}\int_{-\infty}^x e^{-t^2/2}(h(t)-\mathbb Eh(G))\,dt,$ where $G$ has the standard-normal law. On any finite interval, [F2] differentiates the integral term and the product rule differentiates the integrating factor, giving $f'(x)-xf(x)=h(x)-\mathbb Eh(G)$. The total integral of the integrand is zero, so its upper-tail form also holds.

For $x>0$, the upper-tail formula and $0\le h\le1$ give $|f(x)|\le e^{x^2/2}\int_x^\infty e^{-t^2/2}dt=\int_0^\infty e^{-xs-s^2/2}ds\le\min(2,1/x)$. For $x\le0$ the lower-tail formula gives the same bounds. Thus $|xf(x)|\le1$ and the differential equation gives $|f'(x)|\le2$. Away from the two breakpoints of the piecewise-linear $h$, differentiating the Stein equation gives $f''=f+xf'+h'$, so $|f''(x)|\le2+2|x|+\epsilon^{-1}\mathbf1_{[a,a+\epsilon]}(x)$. On any finite segment, split at those breakpoints and apply [F3] on each smooth subinterval to the function $f'$; it is differentiable there, its derivative $f''$ is continuous up to the one-sided endpoints, and hence integrable. Continuity of $f'$ lets the increments add across the breakpoints.

Integrating the last bound along the segment from $x$ to $x+y$ (and using $|f'|\le2$ when $|y|>1$) yields $|f'(x+y)-f'(x)|\le4|y|\left(1+|x|+\epsilon^{-1}\int_0^1\mathbf1_{[a,a+\epsilon]}(x+sy)ds\right).$ For the sum $S_{-i}$ omitting term $i$, its variance is at least $1/2$. After dividing by its standard deviation $\sigma_{-i}\ge1/\sqrt2$, its third-moment sum is at most $\sqrt8r^3<8r^3=(2r)^3$, so the induction definition bounds its CDF error by $\delta_{m-1}(2r)$. Comparing the two endpoints of any interval of length $\epsilon$ with a normal interval, whose density is bounded by one, gives $\Pr\{S_{-i}+sy\in[a,a+\epsilon]\}\le2\epsilon+2\delta_{m-1}(2r)$. Finally, $(\mathbb E|S_{-i}|)^2\le\mathbb E S_{-i}^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_{-i})\le1$, because $\mathbb E(|S_{-i}|-\mathbb E|S_{-i}|)^2\ge0$. Taking expectations in the increment bound therefore gives $\mathbb E|f'(S_{-i}+y)-f'(S_{-i})|\le16|y|(1+\delta_{m-1}(2r)/\epsilon)$.

Integrating by parts on $[-A,A]$ using [F2] gives $\int_{-A}^A f'\varphi= [f\varphi]_{-A}^A+\int_{-A}^Axf\varphi$. The boundary term tends to zero because $f$ is bounded by step 2.1 and $\varphi(A)\to0$ by [F2]; the integrals converge since $f,f'$ are bounded and $|x|\varphi(x)$ is integrable by [F1]. Hence $\mathbb Ef'(G)=\mathbb EGf(G)$. The smoothing inequalities $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,a]}\le h_a\le\mathbf1_{(-\infty,a+\epsilon]}$ show that $\Pr\{S\le a\}-\Phi(a)\le\mathbb Eh_a(S)-\mathbb Eh_a(G)+\epsilon$: the normal mass of an interval of length $\epsilon$ is at most $\epsilon$. For the reverse difference, apply the same calculation to $h_{a-\epsilon}$ and its corresponding Stein solution; the bounds in step 2.1 are uniform in the threshold. For either smoothing function, the Stein equation identifies the expectation difference as $\mathbb E[f'(S)-Sf(S)]$, proving the displayed uniform estimate.

For each $i$, independence and mean zero give $\mathbb E[X_if(S)]=\mathbb E\left[X_i^2\int_0^1 f'(S_{-i}+tX_i)dt\right].$ For the needed moment comparison, write the finite law of $A=|X_i|$ as values $a_j$ with weights $p_j$. For every pair $j,k$, $a_j^2a_k\le(2a_j^3+a_k^3)/3$, since $2a^3+b^3-3a^2b=(a-b)^2(2a+b)\ge0$. Averaging with weights $p_jp_k$ gives $\mathbb E|X_i|^2\,\mathbb E|X_i|\le\mathbb E|X_i|^3$. Using step 3.1 first with increment $tX_i$ and then with increment $X_i$, this inequality yields $|\mathbb E[X_if(S)]-\mathbb E X_i^2\,\mathbb Ef'(S)|\le32\mathbb E|X_i|^3(1+\delta_{m-1}(2r)/\epsilon).$ Summing over $i$ and using $\sum_i\mathbb EX_i^2=1$ bounds the difference in step 3.2 by $32r^3(1+\delta_{m-1}(2r)/\epsilon)$.

Choose $\epsilon=512r^3$. Steps 3.2 and 4.1 give $\delta_m(r)\le544r^3+\tfrac1{16}\delta_{m-1}(2r)$. Inductively, $\delta_{m-1}(2r)\le1088(2r)^3$, so the right side is at most $(544+544)r^3=1088r^3$. For one summand with variance one, Lyapunov gives $r^3\ge\beta\ge1$, and the trivial CDF bound starts the induction. Combining with step 1.2 proves the normalized claim; undoing the variance normalization proves the Statement.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For every $\alpha>0$,

derivations.claim:
Expanding the finite KL sum in [F1] under $P(x)V(y\mid x)$ and grouping the finite terms gives
$$I_P(V)=H(PV)-\sum_xP(x)H(V(\cdot\mid x)).$$
Indeed, the logarithm of the joint-to-product ratio is $\ln V(y\mid x)-\ln(PV)(y)$ on positive joint support; summing the first term gives the negative conditional entropy and summing the second gives the output entropy. Zero-mass coordinates contribute zero by [F1].

For $0<s<t\le1$, [F3] gives $g'(s)=-\ln s-1> -\ln t-1=g'(t)$, since $\ln$ is strictly increasing by its positive derivative and the mean value theorem. If $0<u<v<w\le1$, apply [F4] to $g$ on $[u,v]$ and $[v,w]$. The resulting derivative points satisfy $\xi_1<\xi_2$, so the left secant slope is at least the right secant slope; rearranging is the concavity inequality for $g$ at $v$. Thus $g$ is concave on $(0,1]$.

For $u,w\in[0,1]$ with one endpoint zero, replace that endpoint by a positive sequence tending to zero in the inequality of step 1.2 and use continuity from [F5]. Therefore $g$ is concave on $[0,1]$. $$\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\ln\frac AB.$$

When $A,B>0$, equality holds exactly when $a_i=(A/B)b_i$ for every $i$. If $A>0=B$, both sides are $+\infty$ and no finite equality characterization is asserted.

For probability vectors $P=(p_x)$ and $Q=(q_x)$ on the same finite
nonempty alphabet, their **Kullback–Leibler divergence** (or **relative
entropy**) in the stated direction from $P$ to $Q$ is
$$D(P\|Q):=\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_x\log\frac{p_x}{q_x}.$$
The logarithm is natural. If $p_x>0$ and $q_x=0$ for at least one $x$, set
$D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $p_x=0$, its contribution is zero, including when
$q_x=0$; equivalently, $0\log(0/q_x)=0$. When $P\ll Q$, all ratios in the
sum are positive and finite.

KL formula, including the singular-support case.

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the

Let $W$ be a finite DMC from finite nonempty $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$, with rates and logarithms in nats. For an input law $P$ and $\rho\ge0$, define
$$E_0(\rho,P):=-\ln\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\left(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}P(x)W(y\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}\right)^{1+\rho}.$$
Separately, for $\rho\ge1$, define $B(x,x'):=\sum_y\sqrt{W(y\mid x)W(y\mid x')}$ and
$$E_{0x}(\rho,P):=-\rho\ln\sum_{x,x'}P(x)P(x')B(x,x')^{1/\rho}.$$
For every $a>0$, $0^a=0$; thus zero channel transitions and zero Bhattacharyya coefficients contribute zero to these sums. These are one-letter functions at a fixed $P$; the global maxima and rate-dependent exponent functions are separate definitions.

A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: For any fixed $a>0$, the convention in [F3] extends $t\mapsto t^a$ continuously to $t=0$: given $\epsilon>0$, put $\delta=\exp((\ln\epsilon)/a)>0$. If $0<t<\delta$, monotonicity of $\ln$ gives $a\ln t<\ln\epsilon$, so monotonicity of $\exp$ yields $0<t^a<\epsilon$; at $t=0$ the value is zero. Thus every positive real power used in [F1] is continuous on $[0,\infty)$.

For every $x$, $B(x,x)=\sum_yW(y\mid x)=1$ by [F2]. Thus the inner sum in $E_{0x}$ satisfies
$$\sum_{x,x'}P(x)P(x')B(x,x')^{1/\rho}\ge\sum_xP(x)^2\ge\frac1{|\mathcal X|}>0.$$
The last inequality follows from $|\mathcal X|\sum_xP(x)^2-(\sum_xP(x))^2=\sum_{x<x'}(P(x)-P(x'))^2\ge0$. Every coefficient $B(x,x')^{1/\rho}$ is a fixed finite real, so the inner sum is a continuous polynomial in $P$ and is bounded away from zero; consequently $E_{0x}(\rho,P)$ is real-valued and continuous.

Fix $\rho>0$. Each inner sum $A_y(P)=\sum_xP(x)W(y\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}$ is a continuous nonnegative linear function of $P$. By step 1.1, $A_y(P)^{1+\rho}$ is continuous, so $S(P)=\sum_yA_y(P)^{1+\rho}$ is continuous. For every input law $P$, some $x$ has $P(x)>0$; since row $W(\cdot\mid x)$ sums to one, some $y$ has $W(y\mid x)>0$, giving $A_y(P)>0$ and hence $S(P)>0$. Therefore $E_0(\rho,P)=-\ln S(P)$ is real-valued and continuous. At $\rho=0$, the sum is $\sum_y\sum_xP(x)W(y\mid x)=1$, so $E_0(0,P)=0$.

The finite probability vectors form the nonempty simplex $\Delta=\{P:P(x)\ge0,\sum_xP(x)=1\}$ by [F5]. It is nonempty because a point mass belongs to it; each coordinate lies in $[0,1]$, so it is bounded; and the coordinate inequalities are closed half-spaces while the sum equation is a closed affine hyperplane, so $\Delta$ is closed. Heine–Borel makes $\Delta$ compact, and steps 1.2 and 2.1 show that each objective is continuous and real-valued on it. The extreme-value assertion in [F5] therefore gives an attained finite maximum for every stated $\rho$.

Let $W$ be a finite DMC from finite nonempty $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$, with rates and logarithms in nats. For an input law $P$ and $\rho\ge0$, define
$$E_0(\rho,P):=-\ln\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\left(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}P(x)W(y\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}\right)^{1+\rho}.$$
Separately, for $\rho\ge1$, define $B(x,x'):=\sum_y\sqrt{W(y\mid x)W(y\mid x')}$ and
$$E_{0x}(\rho,P):=-\rho\ln\sum_{x,x'}P(x)P(x')B(x,x')^{1/\rho}.$$
For every $a>0$, $0^a=0$; thus zero channel transitions and zero Bhattacharyya coefficients contribute zero to these sums. These are one-letter functions at a fixed $P$; the global maxima and rate-dependent exponent functions are separate definitions.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For probability vectors $P=(p_x)$ and $Q=(q_x)$ on the same finite
nonempty alphabet, their **Kullback–Leibler divergence** (or **relative
entropy**) in the stated direction from $P$ to $Q$ is
$$D(P\|Q):=\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_x\log\frac{p_x}{q_x}.$$
The logarithm is natural. If $p_x>0$ and $q_x=0$ for at least one $x$, set
$D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $p_x=0$, its contribution is zero, including when
$q_x=0$; equivalently, $0\log(0/q_x)=0$. When $P\ll Q$, all ratios in the
sum are positive and finite.

The generator $f(t)=t\log t$ is admissible for
[[def-finite-f-divergence]] by
[[lem-finite-kl-generator-is-admissible]]. Its boundary values
$f(0)=0$ and $f_\infty=+\infty$ make that f-divergence exactly the displayed
KL formula, including the singular-support case.
For finite probability vectors $p,q$ on the same alphabet, $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$. If $p_i>0=q_i$ for some coordinate, then $D(p\|q)=+\infty$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
For each real $p\ge1$, the function $\phi_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ defined by $\phi_p(t)=|t|^p$ is finite, continuous, Borel measurable and convex. Here $0^p=0$.
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\alpha=(1+\rho)^{-1}\in(0,1)$ and, for an output law $Q$, set $Z_x(Q)=\sum_yW(y\mid x)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha}$. If $Z_x(Q)>0$, define $R_x(y)=W(y\mid x)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha}/Z_x(Q)$. Expanding the finite sums gives for every $V_x\ll W_x$ with finite $D(V_x\|Q)$ $D(V_x\|W_x)+\rho D(V_x\|Q)=(1+\rho)D(V_x\|R_x)-(1+\rho)\ln Z_x(Q).$ By [F3], the minimum over $V_x$ is $-(1+\rho)\ln Z_x(Q)=-\alpha^{-1}\ln Z_x(Q)$. If $Z_x(Q)=0$, every such objective with positive $P(x)$ is infinite, matching the extended value of this expression.

Define $S_y(P)=\sum_xP(x)W(y\mid x)^\alpha$ and $\Psi(P)=\sum_yS_y(P)^{1/\alpha}$. Then [F1] gives $E_0(\rho,P)=-\ln\Psi(P)$. Since $1/\alpha=1+\rho>1$, [F7] shows that each summand $S_y(P)^{1/\alpha}$ is continuous and convex as a function of $P$; hence $\Psi$ is continuous and convex on the input simplex. The simplex is nonempty because it contains a point mass, closed as the intersection of finitely many coordinate half-spaces with the affine equation $\sum_xP(x)=1$, and bounded because every coordinate lies in $[0,1]$. By [F4] it is compact, so $\Psi$ attains a minimum at some $P^*$. For every input law at least one coordinate of $P$ is positive, and that row of $W$ has a positive entry; hence at least one $S_y(P)>0$ and $\Psi(P)>0$. Also, for every $r>0$, $t^r\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta=\varepsilon^{1/r}$; if $0<t<\delta$, strict monotonicity of $\ln$ and $\exp$ gives $t^r<\varepsilon$. Write $S_y=S_y(P^*)$, $\Psi_* =\Psi(P^*)>0$, $T=\{y:S_y>0\}$, and $q^*(y)=S_y^{1/\alpha}/\Psi_*$ on $T$, with $q^*(y)=0$ outside $T$.

For any $V$ and output law $Q$, expansion of finite KL gives $\sum_xP(x)D(V_x\|Q)=I_P(V)+D(PV_Y\|Q)\ge I_P(V),$ with equality at $Q=PV_Y$ by [F2–F3]. Taking the joint infimum over $V,Q$ and applying step 1.1 row by row therefore yields $E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)=\inf_Q\sum_{x:P(x)>0}P(x)f_x(Q),\quad f_x(Q):=-\alpha^{-1}\ln Z_x(Q),$ with $f_x(Q)=+\infty$ when $Z_x(Q)=0.$ Coordinates with $P(x)=0$ are omitted, so no $0\cdot\infty$ term is used.

Put $T_x=\sum_yW(y\mid x)^\alpha S_y^\rho$. For each $x$, move from $P^*$ toward the point mass $\delta_x$ along $P_t=(1-t)P^*+t\delta_x$, so $S_y(P_t)=S_y+t(W(y\mid x)^\alpha-S_y)$. If $S_y>0$, [F5]–[F6] give the derivative of $S_y(P_t)^{1/\alpha}$ at $t=0$ as $\alpha^{-1}S_y^\rho(W(y\mid x)^\alpha-S_y)$. If $S_y=0$, the term equals $t^{1/\alpha}W(y\mid x)$, whose right derivative at zero is zero because $1/\alpha-1=\rho>0$ and the endpoint limit in step 1.2 applies. Therefore the right derivative of $\Psi(P_t)$ at zero is $\alpha^{-1}(T_x-\Psi_*)$, using $\sum_yS_y^{1/\alpha}=\Psi_*$. The minimum at $t=0$ makes this right derivative nonnegative, so $T_x\ge\Psi_*$. Also $\sum_xP^*(x)T_x=\sum_yS_y^{1+\rho}=\Psi_*$. Since every $T_x\ge\Psi_*$ and this weighted average equals $\Psi_*$, equality holds whenever $P^*(x)>0$. Substitution into $Z_x(q^*)=\Psi_*^{-(1-\alpha)}T_x$ gives $Z_x(q^*)\ge\Psi_*^\alpha$, with equality for every active input. Thus $f_x(q^*)\le-\ln\Psi_*$ for all $x$, with equality on $\operatorname{supp}P^*$.

Applying step 2.1 with the particular output law $q^*$ gives, for every $P$, $E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)\le\sum_xP(x)f_x(q^*)\le-\ln\Psi_* =\max_{P'}E_0(\rho,P').$ Therefore $\max_PE_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)\le\max_PE_0(\rho,P)$.

On $[0,\infty)$, the power $t^{1-\alpha}$ is continuous by the endpoint estimate in step 1.2 and concave: on $(0,\infty)$ the second derivative of $-t^{1-\alpha}$ is $(1-\alpha)\alpha t^{-1-\alpha}>0$, so [F5], [F6], and [F8] make $-t^{1-\alpha}$ convex there; continuity extends the concavity inequality to zero. Thus each $Z_x(Q)$ is concave. The function $-\ln z$ is decreasing and convex on $(0,\infty)$, since $\ln$ is increasing by [F9] and $(-\ln z)''=z^{-2}>0$ by [F5], [F6], [F8], and [F10]. Consequently $f_x(Q)=-\alpha^{-1}\ln Z_x(Q)$ is convex wherever $Z_x(Q)>0$: concavity of $Z_x$, monotonicity of $-\ln$, and convexity of $-\ln$ give the convex-combination inequality directly. Hence $F(Q)=\sum_{x:P^*(x)>0}P^*(x)f_x(Q)$ is convex on its finite domain. For $y\in T$, differentiating at the positive point $q^*$ and using $Z_x(q^*)=\Psi_*^\alpha$ for active $x$ from step 2.2 gives $$\frac{\partial F}{\partial Q(y)}(q^*)=-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\frac{\Psi_*^\alpha}{S_y}\frac{\sum_{x:P^*(x)>0}P^*(x)W(y\mid x)^\alpha}{\Psi_*^\alpha}=-\rho.$$ For any strictly positive probability vector $Q$ on $T$, let $g(t)=F((1-t)q^*+tQ)$. It is convex, and $g'_+(0)=\sum_{y\in T}(-\rho)(Q(y)-q^*(y))=0$. Convexity gives $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le g(1)-g(0)$ for $0<t<1$; letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $F(Q)\ge F(q^*)$. If $Q$ has zero coordinates on $T$ but $F(Q)<\infty$, then every active $Z_x(Q)>0$; apply the result to $Q_t=(1-t)Q+tq^*$ and let $t\downarrow0$, using continuity of the finite sums and logarithms on positive $Z_x(Q)$. If $F(Q)=+\infty$, the inequality is immediate. Thus $F(Q)\ge F(q^*)$ for every probability vector supported on $T$.

For a general output law $Q$, let $c=Q(T)$. If $c=0$, every active row has $Z_x(Q)=0$ and $F(Q)=+\infty$. If $c>0$, normalize $Q_T=Q(\cdot\mid T)$. Every active row is supported on $T$, so $Z_x(Q)=c^{1-\alpha}Z_x(Q_T)$ and $f_x(Q)=f_x(Q_T)-\rho\ln c\ge f_x(Q_T)$. Step 3.2 then gives $F(Q)\ge F(q^*)$. Since active inputs satisfy $f_x(q^*)=-\ln\Psi_*$, step 2.1 yields $E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P^*)=F(q^*)=-\ln\Psi_*=\max_PE_0(\rho,P)$.

Step 4.1 gives $\max_PE_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)\ge E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P^*)=\max_PE_0(\rho,P)$, while step 3.1 gives the reverse inequality. This proves the globally optimized identity and establishes no pointwise-in-$P$ equality.

A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.
For a finite DMC $W$ and every $n\ge1$, the block formula $W^n(y^n\mid x^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i)$ is a stochastic kernel from $\mathcal X^n$ to $\mathcal Y^n$.

Given an input law $P_X$, let $Q_{P_X}=P_XW$ be its output law. The **information density** is
$$\imath_{P_X}(x;y):=\ln\frac{W(y\mid x)}{Q_{P_X}(y)}$$
when $P_X(x)W(y\mid x)>0$, and is $-\infty$ otherwise. For block sequences define $\imath_{P_X}(x^n;y^n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\imath_{P_X}(x_i;y_i)$, with any sum containing $-\infty$ equal to $-\infty$. On the support of the induced joint law, both numerator and denominator are positive, and the value is finite.

For a finite DMC $W$, a **length-$n$ code with $M$ messages** is a pair of maps $e:[M]\to\mathcal X^n$ and $d:\mathcal Y^n\to[M]$, where $n,M\ge1$ and $[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$. A message $m$ is encoded as $e(m)$, passed through the block kernel $W^n$ of [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]], and decoded as $d(Y^n)$. The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

For a length-$n$ code $(e,d)$, let
$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
Its **average error** is $\varepsilon_{\rm av}:=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M e_m$, corresponding to a uniform message, and its **maximal error** is $\varepsilon_{\max}:=\max_{1\le m\le M}e_m$.

derivations.claim: Draw codewords $X^n(1),\ldots,X^n(M)$ independently from $P_{X^n}$. Put $Q=P_{X^n}W^n$ and $\tau=\ln((M-1)/2)$. The decoder selects the lowest index $j$ for which $\imath(X^n(j);y^n)>\tau$; if no index passes, it outputs message $1$. This defines a deterministic code decoder for each realized codebook.

If message $j$ is sent, an error can occur only if its own test fails or an earlier codeword passes. Thus its conditional error is at most $\Pr[\imath(X^n(j);Y^n)\le\tau\mid X^n(j)]+\sum_{k<j}\Pr[\imath(X^n(k);Y^n)>\tau\mid X^n(j)].$ The first probability averaged over the true codeword and output is $\Pr_{P_{X^n}W^n}[\imath\le\tau]$. Each earlier independent codeword and the true output have law $P_{X^n}\otimes Q$, so its averaged term is $\Pr_{P_{X^n}\otimes Q}[\imath>\tau]$.

Averaging over the uniform message index gives ensemble-average error at most $\Pr_{P_{X^n}W^n}[\imath\le\tau]+\frac{M-1}{2}\Pr_{P_{X^n}\otimes Q}[\imath>\tau],$ because $M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M(j-1)=(M-1)/2$. On the event $\imath>\tau$, the likelihood ratio identity gives $\Pr_{P\otimes Q}[\imath>\tau]=\mathbb E_{PW}[e^{-\imath}\mathbf1_{\{\imath>\tau\}}]$. Therefore this bound equals $\mathbb E_{PW}[e^{-(\imath-\tau)_+}]$.

The finite random codebook ensemble has some realization whose average error is no larger than its expectation; otherwise every realization would exceed the ensemble average. With $\tau=\ln((M-1)/2)$, this realization proves the stated bound. A one-message code has no decoding error.

Let $P,Q$ be probability vectors on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$
([[def-finite-probability-vector]]). They define finite probability spaces
with outcome weights $p_x$ and $q_x$, respectively
([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). For $h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, write
$E_Ph:=\sum_xp_xh(x)$ and $E_Qh:=\sum_xq_xh(x)$; these are the finite
expectations ([[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]]). Test the
simple null $H_0:P$ against the simple alternative $H_1:Q$. A randomized test is a function
$\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $\phi(x)$ is the probability of rejecting
$H_0$ after observing $x$; thus $1-\phi(x)$ is the probability of accepting
$H_0$ ([[def-randomized-test]]). Its type-I error is
$\sum_xp_x\phi(x)$, and its type-II error is
$\sum_xq_x(1-\phi(x))$ ([[def-test-size-and-power]]).

For $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, define the oriented type-II testing function
$$\beta_\epsilon(P,Q):=\inf_{\substack{\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]\\\sum_xp_x\phi(x)\le\epsilon}}\sum_xq_x(1-\phi(x)).$$
Here the first argument is the null law and the second is the alternative
law; $\epsilon$ bounds rejection under the first law, while the objective is
acceptance of the null under the second. The feasible set is nonempty because
$\phi=0$ is allowed, and every objective value lies in $[0,1]$. Thus the set
of objective values is nonempty and bounded below in $\mathbb R$, so it has a
real infimum: [[def-real-numbers]] identifies $\mathbb R$ with the
Cauchy-sequence reals, [[thm-reals-ordered-field]] gives their ordered-field
structure, and [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] gives their
least-upper-bound property. [[def-complete-ordered-field]] gives the
equivalent infimum property. Since the set also lies in $[0,1]$, that
infimum lies in $[0,1]$. In the
Neyman–Pearson-region convention that constrains null acceptance below by
$\gamma$, this is the lower boundary value at $\gamma=1-\epsilon$.

Under $\widetilde Q$, its type-II error is $\mathbb E_{\widetilde Q}(1-\phi)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\sum_{y^n}Q_{Y^n}(y^n)\mathbf1\{d(y^n)=m\}=\frac1M,$ since for each output exactly one message is decoded. citations.quote:
A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

For a finite DMC $W$, a **length-$n$ code with $M$ messages** is a pair of maps $e:[M]\to\mathcal X^n$ and $d:\mathcal Y^n\to[M]$, where $n,M\ge1$ and $[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$. A message $m$ is encoded as $e(m)$, passed through the block kernel $W^n$ of [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]], and decoded as $d(Y^n)$. The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

For a length-$n$ code $(e,d)$, let
$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
Its **average error** is $\varepsilon_{\rm av}:=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M e_m$, corresponding to a uniform message, and its **maximal error** is $\varepsilon_{\max}:=\max_{1\le m\le M}e_m$.

Let $W$ be a finite unconstrained DMC from finite nonempty $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$, with rates and logarithms in nats. The one-letter function $E_0(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge0$ and $E_{0x}(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge1$ are defined in [[def-it-one-letter-gallager-exponent-functions]]. Their maxima over the input simplex are attained and finite by [[lem-it-gallager-input-maxima-attained]]. For every $\rho\ge0$, define $E_0(\rho):=\max_P E_0(\rho,P)$; on the random-coding range set
$$E_r(R):=\sup_{0\le\rho\le1}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
The expurgated function and sphere-packing expression are
$$E_{\rm ex}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge1}\left\{\max_P E_{0x}(\rho,P)-\rho R\right\},\qquad E_{\rm sp}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge0}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
These functions define lower or upper bounds used on this page; they do not assert that an error-exponent limit exists or that the sphere-packing bound applies without its later strict-feasibility hypothesis.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

Fix $r\in(0,1]$. If $r=1$, $(a+b)^r=a^r+b^r$. If $0<r<1$, then $u\mapsto u^{r-1}$ has derivative $(r-1)u^{r-2}<0$ on $(0,\infty)$ by [F4], so it is nonincreasing by [F5]. For $t>0$, put $g(t)=1+t^r-(1+t)^r$; [F4] gives $g'(t)=r(t^{r-1}-(1+t)^{r-1})\ge0$. Also $t^r\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: its derivative is positive, and for any $\eta>0$, $0<t<\eta^{1/r}$ gives $t^r<\eta$ by [F4]–[F5]. Thus $g$ extends continuously to $g(0)=0$. By [F5] on $[0,\infty)$, $g(t)\ge0$ for all $t\ge0$. If $a>0$, scale with $t=b/a$ and use [F4] to obtain $(a+b)^r\le a^r+b^r$; if $a=0$, equality holds, including $a=b=0$. Induction gives $(\sum_j a_j)^r\le\sum_j a_j^r$ for every finite nonnegative family (the empty family gives $0=0$). Now draw $M'$ codewords independently from $P^n$ and take $r=1/\rho$ for $\rho\ge1$. The proved finite-sum inequality and step 1.1 yield $\mathbb E f_m^{1/\rho}\le\sum_{j\ne m}\mathbb E B^n(X_m^n,X_j^n)^{1/\rho}=(M'-1)\left(\sum_{x,x'}P(x)P(x')B(x,x')^{1/\rho}\right)^n.$ The equality follows from independent coordinates, the product form of $B^n$, and the power laws in [F4].

Averaging [2.1] over messages and codebooks gives a codebook with $M'^{-1}\sum_m f_m^{1/\rho}\le(M'-1)z^n$, where $z=\sum_{x,x'}P(x)P(x')B(x,x')^{1/\rho}$. At least $M'/2$ messages satisfy $f_m^{1/\rho}\le2(M'-1)z^n$; otherwise their sum would exceed $M'(M'-1)z^n$. Restrict the code to $M'/2$ such messages, using ML decoding among the retained words. Removing competitors cannot increase their ML error, so maximal error is at most $[2(M'-1)z^n]^\rho$.

Set $M'=2M_n$, retain exactly $M_n$ messages, and take $-n^{-1}\ln$ of the bound in step 3.1. Since $n^{-1}\ln(M'-1)\to R$, this gives $E^-_{\rm max}(R)\ge -\rho\ln z-\rho R=E_{0x}(\rho,P)-\rho R$. Optimizing over $P$ and $\rho\ge1$ proves the maximal-error bound. Average error is no larger than maximal error for the same code, so its liminf exponent satisfies the same lower bound.

A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

For a finite DMC $W$, a **length-$n$ code with $M$ messages** is a pair of maps $e:[M]\to\mathcal X^n$ and $d:\mathcal Y^n\to[M]$, where $n,M\ge1$ and $[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$. A message $m$ is encoded as $e(m)$, passed through the block kernel $W^n$ of [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]], and decoded as $d(Y^n)$. The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

For a length-$n$ code $(e,d)$, let
$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
Its **average error** is $\varepsilon_{\rm av}:=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M e_m$, corresponding to a uniform message, and its **maximal error** is $\varepsilon_{\max}:=\max_{1\le m\le M}e_m$.

Let $W$ be a finite unconstrained DMC from finite nonempty $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$, with rates and logarithms in nats. The one-letter function $E_0(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge0$ and $E_{0x}(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge1$ are defined in [[def-it-one-letter-gallager-exponent-functions]]. Their maxima over the input simplex are attained and finite by [[lem-it-gallager-input-maxima-attained]]. For every $\rho\ge0$, define $E_0(\rho):=\max_P E_0(\rho,P)$; on the random-coding range set
$$E_r(R):=\sup_{0\le\rho\le1}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
The expurgated function and sphere-packing expression are
$$E_{\rm ex}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge1}\left\{\max_P E_{0x}(\rho,P)-\rho R\right\},\qquad E_{\rm sp}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge0}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
These functions define lower or upper bounds used on this page; they do not assert that an error-exponent limit exists or that the sphere-packing bound applies without its later strict-feasibility hypothesis.

Let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex. If $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in I$, and $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i=1$, then

$$f\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i f(x_i).$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in I$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the point $\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y$ belongs to $I$. The function $f$ is **convex** when the convex-combination inequality holds for every weight in $[0,1]$:

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

It is **strictly convex** when this inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<\lambda<1$. It is **concave** (respectively **strictly concave**) when $-f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). It is **midpoint convex** when the displayed inequality is required only at $\lambda=1/2$.
Every length-$n$ code with average error $\varepsilon_{\rm av}$ has a subcode with at least $M/2$ messages and maximal error at most $2\varepsilon_{\rm av}$.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For an input probability vector $P_X$ on $\mathcal X$ ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]), let $P_{XY}(x,y):=P_X(x)W(y\mid x)$ and $Q_{P_X}(y):=\sum_xP_X(x)W(y\mid x)$. Write $I(P_X;W):=I(X;Y)$ for this joint law, using [[def-it-finite-mutual-information]]. The **single-letter information capacity** is
$$C(W):=\sup_{P_X} I(P_X;W),$$
measured in nats per channel use. The finite-dimensional maximum is attained, as proved in [[lem-discrete-memoryless-channel-capacity-is-attained]].
For every finite DMC $W$, the supremum $C(W)$ is a maximum: there is an input probability vector $P_X^*$ such that $I(P_X^*;W)=C(W)$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

derivations.claim: Fix $0<\rho\le1$, an input law $P$, and an $M$-word codebook drawn independently from $P^n$. Use maximum-likelihood decoding with the lowest-index tie rule. If message $m$ is sent and $y^n$ is received with $W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)>0$, an error implies some competitor has likelihood at least the true likelihood. Hence its error indicator is at most $\left(\sum_{j\ne m}\left[\frac{W^n(y^n\mid x_j^n)}{W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)}\right]^{1/(1+\rho)}\right)^\rho,$ which is at least one on every error event; outputs of zero true likelihood carry no channel mass.

For fixed $P$, write $A_y(\rho)=\sum_xP(x)W(y\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}$ and $S(\rho)=\sum_yA_y(\rho)^{1+\rho}$. If $W(y\mid x)>0$, [F7]–[F8] and the chain rule give $\left.\frac{d}{d\rho}W(y\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}\right|_{\rho=0}=-W(y\mid x)\ln W(y\mid x)$; if $W(y\mid x)=0$, that term is identically zero. Thus, for $q_y=A_y(0)=(PW)(y)>0$, $$A_y'(0)=-\sum_{x:W(y\mid x)>0}P(x)W(y\mid x)\ln W(y\mid x).$$ On a neighborhood of $0$ where $A_y(\rho)>0$, write $A_y(\rho)^{1+\rho}=\exp((1+\rho)\ln A_y(\rho))$. By [F7]–[F8] and the product and chain rules, its derivative at zero is $q_y\ln q_y+A_y'(0)$. If $q_y=0$, every $P(x)W(y\mid x)=0$, so $A_y(\rho)=0$ for all $\rho\ge0$ and its outer term vanishes identically. Summing the finite terms gives $$S'(0)=\sum_{y:q_y>0}q_y\ln q_y-\sum_{x,y:P(x)W(y\mid x)>0}P(x)W(y\mid x)\ln W(y\mid x)=-I(P,W),$$ because [F5] expands $I(P,W)=\sum_{x,y:PW>0}P(x)W(y\mid x)\ln\frac{W(y\mid x)}{q_y}$. Since $S(0)=1$ and $E_0(\rho,P)=-\ln S(\rho)$, the right derivative is $\partial_\rho E_0(0,P)=I(P,W)$.

Fix $0<\rho\le1$. By [F8], the function $h(t)=-t^\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$ has $h''(t)=\rho(1-\rho)t^{\rho-2}\ge0$, so [F10] makes it convex there (for $\rho=1$ it is affine). The positive derivative $\rho t^{\rho-1}$ and [F11] make $t^\rho$ increasing. Given $\eta>0$, put $\delta=\eta^{1/\rho}$; if $0<t<\delta$, then $0<t^\rho<\delta^\rho=\eta$ by [F11]. Thus $t^\rho$ extends continuously to zero with value zero. For nonnegative $x,y$ and a weight $\lambda\in[0,1]$, apply the convexity inequality for $h$ to $x+u,y+u>0$ and let $u\downarrow0$; continuity extends it to $[0,\infty)$. Applying finite convex Jensen [F3] to this $h$ and the values of any finite nonnegative random variable $Z$ gives $-(\mathbb EZ)^\rho\le-\mathbb E Z^\rho$, or $\mathbb E Z^\rho\le(\mathbb EZ)^\rho$. This includes $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\rho=1$ without a zero-to-zero power convention.

Conditional on $x_m^n,y^n$, the power Jensen inequality from step 1.3 bounds the expected $\rho$-power by the $\rho$-power of its mean. Independence of each competitor gives that mean as $(M-1)\frac{A_n(y^n)}{W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)^{1/(1+\rho)}},\qquad A_n(y^n):=\sum_{x^n}P^n(x^n)W^n(y^n\mid x^n)^{1/(1+\rho)}.$ Multiplication by the true likelihood changes its power to $1-\rho/(1+\rho)=1/(1+\rho)$. Averaging over the transmitted word and summing over outputs therefore bounds ensemble average error by $(M-1)^\rho\sum_{y^n}A_n(y^n)^{1+\rho}.$

The product law in [F1] makes $A_n(y^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_xP(x)W(y_i\mid x)^{1/(1+\rho)}$. Thus the sum in step 2.1 factors into the $n$th power of the single-letter sum defining $E_0(\rho,P)$ in [F2]. Some deterministic codebook has average error at most its ensemble mean, so for each $n$ a code exists with $\epsilon_{\rm av}\le\exp\{-n[E_0(\rho,P)-\rho n^{-1}\ln(M-1)]\}.$

With $M_n=\lceil e^{nR}\rceil$, one has $n^{-1}\ln(M_n-1)\to R$. Taking the liminf exponent in step 3.1 and optimizing over $P$ and $0<\rho\le1$ gives the corresponding positive-parameter supremum. For a capacity-achieving $P^*$ from [F6], each $A_y(\rho)$ tends to $q_y=(P^*W)(y)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$. If $q_y>0$, then $A_y(\rho)^{1+\rho}=\exp((1+\rho)\ln A_y(\rho))\to q_y$; if $q_y=0$, all $P^*(x)W(y\mid x)=0$ and that term is identically zero. Hence $S(\rho)\to\sum_yq_y=1$ and $E_0(\rho,P^*)=-\ln S(\rho)\to0$ by [F9]. Since $E_0(\rho)\ge E_0(\rho,P^*)$, the positive-parameter supremum is at least $\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}(E_0(\rho,P^*)-\rho R)=0$. The added endpoint $\rho=0$ has value zero, so it does not change the supremum, which is $E_r(R)$.

Apply the same bound at size $2M_n$ and then [F4]. The retained code has at least $M_n$ messages, so selecting exactly $M_n$ messages leaves maximal error at most twice the old average error. The factor two and the rate difference $n^{-1}\ln(2M_n)-R\to0$ do not change the liminf exponent. Hence $E^-_{\rm max}(R)\ge E_r(R)$.
If $R<C(W)$, choose a maximizing $P^*$ by [F6]. Step 1.2 gives $E_0(\rho,P^*)-\rho R=\rho(C(W)-R)+o(\rho)>0$ for sufficiently small $\rho>0$. The supremum defining $E_r(R)$ is therefore positive.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
