Let $X$ take values in an alphabet $\mathcal X$ of size $m\ge2$, let $Y$ be finite, and let $\widehat X$ be an estimator in the same alphabet generated from $Y$, so the joint pmf factors as $p_{XY\widehat X}=p_{XY}p_{\widehat X|Y}$. Put $P_e=\mathbb P[\widehat X\ne X]$ and define

$$h_2(t):=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t),\qquad 0\ln0:=0.$$

Then

$$H(X|Y)\le h_2(P_e)+P_e\ln(m-1)\le \ln2+P_e\ln m.$$

For $m=1$, $X$ is constant and $H(X|Y)=0$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.
For finite probability vectors $p,q$ on the same alphabet, $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$. If $p_i>0=q_i$ for some coordinate, then $D(p\|q)=+\infty$.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

Let $(a_i)_{i=1}^n,(b_i)_{i=1}^n$ be finite nonnegative real vectors, with $A=\sum_i a_i$ and $B=\sum_i b_i$. Interpret $\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln(a_i/b_i)$ as $+\infty$ if some $a_i>0=b_i$; otherwise zero coordinates contribute $0$. Interpret $A\ln(A/B)$ as $0$ if $A=0$ and as $+\infty$ if $A>0=B$. Then

$$\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\ln\frac AB.$$

When $A,B>0$, equality holds exactly when $a_i=(A/B)b_i$ for every $i$. If $A>0=B$, both sides are $+\infty$ and no finite equality characterization is asserted.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, disjoint, and convex. Then there is $a\ne0$ such that

$$\langle a,c\rangle\le\langle a,d\rangle\qquad(c\in C,\ d\in D).$$

Thus $C$ and $D$ are separated by a hyperplane in the sense of [[def-supporting-hyperplane-to-a-convex-set]]. The inequality need not be strict when the two sets have distance zero.

Let $W$ be a finite DMC. For each $\rho>0$ and input law $P$, define
$$E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P):=\inf_{V:\,V(\cdot\mid x)\ll W(\cdot\mid x)}\left\{\sum_xP(x)D(V(\cdot\mid x)\|W(\cdot\mid x))+\rho I_P(V)\right\},$$
where $V$ ranges over row-stochastic channels on the same alphabets, $I_P(V)$ is the mutual information of $P(x)V(y\mid x)$, and terms with $P(x)=0$ are omitted. At $\rho=0$, set $E_{0,\rm cc}(0,P)=0$. Then
$$\max_P E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)=\max_P E_0(\rho,P),$$
with $E_0$ from [[def-it-gallager-and-expurgated-exponent-functions]]. This equality holds for every $\rho>0$ and is after optimizing over $P$; it is not asserted for each fixed $P$. At $\rho=0$, both sides are zero under the stated conventions.

Let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex. If $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in I$, and $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i=1$, then

$$f\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i f(x_i).$$

For a finite DMC $W$, $R>0$, and $n\ge1$, set $M_n=\lceil e^{nR}\rceil$. Let $P_k^*(n,M_n)$ be the minimum error probability among length-$n$ deterministic codes of that size under criterion $k\in\{\mathrm{av},\mathrm{max}\}$, where the two errors are those of [[def-fixed-length-channel-code-errors]]. This minimum exists because the encoder and decoder range over finite sets. Define
$$E_k^-(R):=\liminf_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln P_k^*(n,M_n),\qquad E_k^+(R):=\limsup_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln P_k^*(n,M_n),$$
with $-\ln0=+\infty$. An error-exponent limit $E_k(R)$ is used only when the liminf and limsup agree in the extended reals. These are exponents of error probability; the exponent of success probability is a different quantity. No general exact formula for the finite-DMC reliability function is part of this definition.

Let $W$ be a finite unconstrained DMC from finite nonempty $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$, with rates and logarithms in nats. The one-letter function $E_0(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge0$ and $E_{0x}(\rho,P)$ for $\rho\ge1$ are defined in [[def-it-one-letter-gallager-exponent-functions]]. Their maxima over the input simplex are attained and finite by [[lem-it-gallager-input-maxima-attained]]. For every $\rho\ge0$, define $E_0(\rho):=\max_P E_0(\rho,P)$; on the random-coding range set
$$E_r(R):=\sup_{0\le\rho\le1}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
The expurgated function and sphere-packing expression are
$$E_{\rm ex}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge1}\left\{\max_P E_{0x}(\rho,P)-\rho R\right\},\qquad E_{\rm sp}(R):=\sup_{\rho\ge0}\{E_0(\rho)-\rho R\}.$$
These functions define lower or upper bounds used on this page; they do not assert that an error-exponent limit exists or that the sphere-packing bound applies without its later strict-feasibility hypothesis.

For every $\alpha>0$,
$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\log x}{x^\alpha}=0.$$

Let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ be finite nonempty sets and let $V(y\mid x)$ be a row-stochastic channel. For an input probability vector $P$, write $I_P(V)$ for the mutual information under the joint law $P(x)V(y\mid x)$. Then $P\mapsto I_P(V)$ is concave: for input laws $P_0,P_1$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$I_{\lambda P_0+(1-\lambda)P_1}(V)\ge\lambda I_{P_0}(V)+(1-\lambda)I_{P_1}(V).$$

derivations.claim: The allowed $V$ form a compact product of row simplexes. For fixed $P$, $I_P(V)$ and $D_P(V)$ are continuous in $V$: finite sums use $t\ln t\to0$ at zero by [F12], and every denominator $W(y\mid x)$ charged by $V$ is a fixed positive transition. Thus $J(P)=\min_V I_P(V)$ exists. The joint map $(P,V)\mapsto I_P(V)$ is continuous on the compact product of the input simplex and the allowed-channel set; [F7] makes it uniformly continuous. Therefore $|J(P)-J(P')|\le\sup_V|I_P(V)-I_{P'}(V)|\to0$ as $P'\to P$. The continuous $J$ attains its finite maximum $R_\infty$ by [F7]. Since finite mutual information is nonnegative by [F4], $J(P)\ge0$ and $R_\infty\ge0$. Since $R>R_\infty$, for every $P$ its minimizing channel $V_0$ satisfies $I_P(V_0)=J(P)<R$.

Consider any deterministic $M\ge2$ message code whose every codeword has type $P$, and evaluate its average error $e_V$ through the product channel $V^n$. Let $U$ be its uniform message and $X^n$ its codeword. Since $X^n$ is a function of $U$ and the channel depends on $U$ only through $X^n$, $I(U;Y^n)=H(Y^n)-H(Y^n\mid U)$. The finite entropy chain rule and nonnegative conditional mutual information in [F4] give $H(Y^n)\le\sum_iH(Y_i)$. The product-channel law in [F1] gives $H(Y^n\mid U)=\sum_iH(Y_i\mid X_i)$, so $I(U;Y^n)\le\sum_iI(X_i;Y_i)=\sum_i I_{P_i}(V)$, where $P_i$ is the law of $X_i$ under the uniform message. Every codeword has type $P$, hence $n^{-1}\sum_iP_i=P$. Concavity [F13] and finite Jensen [F10] imply $I(U;Y^n)\le nI_P(V)$. Fano's inequality [F3] now yields
$$e_V\ge1-\frac{nI_P(V)+\ln2}{\ln M}.$$
The entropy formula [F5] and limit [F12] also show that $P\mapsto I_P(V)$ is continuous, as needed when types vary.

For fixed $P$, the closed feasible set $\{V:I_P(V)\le R\}$ is nonempty and compact, so $S_P(R):=\min_{I_P(V)\le R}D_P(V)$ exists. The open infimum over $I_P(V)<R$ equals this minimum: if $V^*$ minimizes the closed problem, mix it with the strict witness $V_0$ from step 1.1. Convexity of $I_P$ gives $I_P((1-t)V^*+tV_0)<R$ for $t>0$, while continuity gives $D_P((1-t)V^*+tV_0)\to S_P(R)$. For $D_P$, [F6] gives convexity row by row and then after the finite $P$-weighted sum. For $I_P$, write it as $D(PV_{XY}\|P\otimes PV_Y)$; both arguments are the same convex mixtures when $V$ is mixed, so [F6] gives convexity. This proves the required convexity and continuity facts.

For each row $x$, under $V(\cdot\mid x)$ the log ratio $\ln[V(Y\mid x)/W(Y\mid x)]$ has mean $D(V_x\|W_x)$ and variance bounded uniformly over allowed $V$: the finite set of positive $W(y\mid x)$ has a positive minimum, and $t(\ln(t/W(y\mid x)))^2$ extends continuously at $t=0$. Thus for some finite $K_W$, a codeword of type $P_n$ has log ratio $L=\ln[V^n(Y^n\mid x^n)/W^n(Y^n\mid x^n)]$ with mean $nD_{P_n}(V)$ and variance at most $nK_W$. On $L>n(D_{P_n}(V)+\eta)$, the squared centered deviation exceeds $n^2\eta^2$, so the event indicator is at most $(L-\mathbb E L)^2/(n^2\eta^2)$. Taking expectations gives $V^n\{L>n(D_{P_n}(V)+\eta)\}\le K_W/(n\eta^2)$. On its complement $W^n\ge e^{-n(D_{P_n}(V)+\eta)}V^n$; integrating over decoder error events gives $e_W\ge e^{-n(D_{P_n}(V)+\eta)}\left(e_V-\frac{K_W}{n\eta^2}\right).$

At each $n$, choose a code attaining the finite-block minimum average error. For any such code of size $M_n$, partition its messages into input types; there are at most $(n+1)^{|\mathcal X|}$ types. Restrict to a largest type class of size $M'_n\ge M_n/(n+1)^{|\mathcal X|}$. Reindex the retained messages and map every old decoder output outside the retained class to one fixed retained message. For each retained message this decoder cannot increase its error, so if $e_n$ is the original average error and $e'_n$ the restricted one, then $e_n\ge(M'_n/M_n)e'_n$. Since $M_n=\lceil e^{nR}\rceil$ and $R>0$ by step 1.1, $M'_n$ grows exponentially and $n^{-1}\ln M'_n\to R$ by [F12]. Along any subsequence realizing the limsup exponent, compactness gives a further subsequence of selected types $P_n\to P$. For each allowed $V$ with $I_P(V)<R$, continuity from step 1.2 makes its Fano lower bound bounded away from zero; step 2.2 then gives $\limsup -n^{-1}\ln e_n\le D_P(V)+\eta$, since the type-class factor costs only $|\mathcal X|\ln(n+1)/n$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ and taking the infimum over strict-feasible $V$ proves $E^+_{\rm av}(R)\le\sup_P\inf_{V:I_P(V)<R}D_P(V)=\sup_PS_P(R),$ where the equality is step 2.1. Since every code's maximal error is at least its average error, $P^*_{\rm max}(n,M_n)\ge P^*_{\rm av}(n,M_n)$ and the same upper bound holds for $E^+_{\rm max}$.

Fix $P$. Form the upper image $G=\{(a,b):a\ge I_P(V),\ b\ge D_P(V)\text{ for some allowed }V\}$ and the open convex set $O=(-\infty,R)\times(-\infty,S_P(R))$. They are nonempty convex sets. If a point lay in both, its witnessing $V$ would satisfy $I_P(V)<R$ and $D_P(V)<S_P(R)$, contradicting the definition of the closed minimum; hence they are disjoint. Convexity of $G$ follows from step 2.1. Apply [F8] under [A1] to obtain a nonzero normal separating $G$ from $O$. Because $G$ is upper in each coordinate, the separating normal in the orientation $a\cdot g\le a\cdot o$ must have nonpositive coordinates (otherwise increasing that coordinate of $g$ violates separation). Reversing its sign gives weights $u,v\ge0$, not both zero, with $uI_P(V)+vD_P(V)\ge uR+vS_P(R)\quad\text{for every allowed }V.$ Strict feasibility from step 1.1 forces $v>0$: if $v=0$, then $u>0$ and the inequality contradicts $I_P(V_0)<R$. Normalize $v=1$ and put $\rho=u/v\ge0$.

The separator gives $\inf_V\{D_P(V)+\rho I_P(V)\}-\rho R\ge S_P(R)$. Conversely, a minimizer $V^*$ of the closed problem has $I_P(V^*)\le R$ and $D_P(V^*)=S_P(R)$, so for every $\rho\ge0$, $\inf_V\{D_P(V)+\rho I_P(V)\}-\rho R\le S_P(R).$ Thus strict feasibility proves the exact dual identity $S_P(R)=\sup_{\rho\ge0}\left\{E_{0,\rm cc}(\rho,P)-\rho R\right\},$ with $E_{0,\rm cc}(0,P)=0$.

Taking suprema over $P$ and $\rho$ in step 4.1, interchanging two suprema, and applying [F9] for $\rho>0$ (at $\rho=0$ both optimized quantities are zero) gives $\sup_PS_P(R)=\sup_{\rho\ge0}\{\max_PE_0(\rho,P)-\rho R\}=E_{\rm sp}(R).$ Combining with step 3.1 proves both stated converses. The strict condition $R>R_\infty$ was used in steps 1.1, 2.1, and 4.1; no endpoint conclusion follows from this proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.
For a finite DMC $W$ and every $n\ge1$, the block formula $W^n(y^n\mid x^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i)$ is a stochastic kernel from $\mathcal X^n$ to $\mathcal Y^n$.
For every finite DMC $W$, the supremum $C(W)$ is a maximum: there is an input probability vector $P_X^*$ such that $I(P_X^*;W)=C(W)$.

For an input probability vector $P_X$ on $\mathcal X$ ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]), let $P_{XY}(x,y):=P_X(x)W(y\mid x)$ and $Q_{P_X}(y):=\sum_xP_X(x)W(y\mid x)$. Write $I(P_X;W):=I(X;Y)$ for this joint law, using [[def-it-finite-mutual-information]]. The **single-letter information capacity** is
$$C(W):=\sup_{P_X} I(P_X;W),$$
measured in nats per channel use. The finite-dimensional maximum is attained, as proved in [[lem-discrete-memoryless-channel-capacity-is-attained]].
For a finite DMC $W$, every input law attaining $C(W)=\max_P I(P,W)$ induces the same output law $Q^*$. This output law is unique even when the capacity-achieving input law is not.

Let $P_X^*$ attain $C(W)$ and let $Q^*:=P_X^*W$. If $W(y\mid x)>0$, then $Q^*(y)>0$, and for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
$$D(W(\cdot\mid x)\|Q^*)\le C(W).$$

For every finite DMC, the set $\Pi(W)$ of capacity-achieving input laws is nonempty and compact, and the function $P\mapsto V(P,W)$ is continuous on $\Pi(W)$. Therefore $V_{\min}(W)$ and $V_{\max}(W)$ in [[def-it-channel-dispersion]] are attained.

Let $P$ be an input probability vector for the finite DMC $W$, and let $P_Y(y)=\sum_xP(x)W(y\mid x)$. On cells with $P(x)W(y\mid x)>0$, define $\imath_P(x;y)=\ln[W(y\mid x)/P_Y(y)]$; the denominator is then positive. Put
$$V(P,W):=\sum_{x:P(x)>0}P(x)\operatorname{Var}_{W(\cdot\mid x)}[\imath_P(x;Y)].$$
Let $C(W)=\max_P I(P,W)$ and $\Pi(W)=\{P:I(P,W)=C(W)\}$, the nonempty set of capacity-achieving input distributions. Define
$$V_{\min}(W):=\min_{P\in\Pi(W)}V(P,W),\qquad V_{\max}(W):=\max_{P\in\Pi(W)}V(P,W).$$
The local attainment lemma [[lem-it-dmc-dispersion-attains-minimum]] proves these extrema exist. Dispersion is measured in nats squared. In the normal-approximation theorem on this page only the fixed range $0<\epsilon<1/2$ and premise $V_{\min}(W)>0$ are used.

For every CAID $P\in\Pi(W)$, let $Q^*=PW$ and let $(X,Y)\sim P(x)W(y\mid x)$. For every $x$ with $P(x)>0$,
$$\mathbb E[\ln(W(Y\mid x)/Q^*(Y))\mid X=x]=C(W),$$
and
$$\operatorname{Var}[\ln(W(Y\mid X)/Q^*(Y))]=V(P,W).$$

Let $W$ be a finite DMC, $C=C(W)$, and $\Pi=\{P:I(P,W)=C\}$. There is $\alpha>0$, depending on $W$, such that every input law $P$ satisfies
$$C-I(P,W)\ge\alpha\,\operatorname{dist}_2(P,\Pi)^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent, finite-support real random variables with $\mathbb E X_i=0$ and total variance $\sigma^2=\sum_i\mathbb E X_i^2>0$. If $S=\sum_iX_i$ and $\Phi$ is the standard-normal CDF, then
$$\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}\left|\Pr\{S/\sigma\le z\}-\Phi(z)\right|\le1088\,\frac{\sum_i\mathbb E|X_i|^3}{\sigma^3}.$$

Let $W^n$ be the block channel of a finite DMC, let $P_{X^n}$ be any input law, and let $M\ge2$. Define the charged information density $\imath(x^n;y^n)=\ln[W^n(y^n\mid x^n)/(P_{X^n}W^n)(y^n)]$ on the support of $P_{X^n}W^n$. There is a deterministic length-$n$ code with $M$ messages and average error at most
$$\mathbb E\exp\left(-\left[\imath(X^n;Y^n)-\ln\frac{M-1}{2}\right]_+\right),$$
where $(X^n,Y^n)\sim P_{X^n}W^n$. For $M=1$, a zero-error code exists. The conclusion is an average-error bound and does not by itself bound every message's error.

For a finite DMC $W$, a **length-$n$ code with $M$ messages** is a pair of maps $e:[M]\to\mathcal X^n$ and $d:\mathcal Y^n\to[M]$, where $n,M\ge1$ and $[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$. A message $m$ is encoded as $e(m)$, passed through the block kernel $W^n$ of [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]], and decoded as $d(Y^n)$. The encoder and decoder are deterministic; there is no feedback, and no input-cost constraint is imposed.

For a length-$n$ code $(e,d)$, let
$$e_m:=W^n\{y^n:d(y^n)\ne m\mid e(m)\}.$$
Its **average error** is $\varepsilon_{\rm av}:=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M e_m$, corresponding to a uniform message, and its **maximal error** is $\varepsilon_{\max}:=\max_{1\le m\le M}e_m$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Z$ have the standard normal law and let
$\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ be its cumulative distribution function. Then $\Phi$ is
continuous and strictly increasing, with limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and
$+\infty$, and $P(Z=x)=0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$. For each $q\in(0,1)$
there is a unique real $z_q$ with
$\Phi(z_q)=q$, and
$$z_{1-q}=-z_q.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every $\alpha>0$,
$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\log x}{x^\alpha}=0.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

derivations.claim: Choose any CAID and let $Q^*$ be its output law. By [F3], every row is supported on $Q^*$ and has divergence $d_x:=D(W_x\|Q^*)\le C(W)$. For every CAID $P$, [F5] gives $\mathbb E[\imath_P(X;Y)\mid X=x]=C(W)$ on each positive-mass input and $\operatorname{Var}(\imath_P(X;Y))=V(P,W)$.

The set $\Pi(W)$ is compact by finite-simplex compactness and continuity of $I(P,W)$, and [F4] supplies a minimum-dispersion CAID. Since $Q^*$ is positive on every globally reachable output, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $\Pi(W)$ in which every $(PW)(y)$ on that support is bounded below by a positive constant. On $U$, the finite formulas for $V(P,W)$ and $T(P,W):=\sum_xP(x)\mathbb E_{W_x}|\imath_P(x;Y)-D(W_x\|PW)|^3$ are smooth functions of $P$ with bounded derivatives. Shrinking $U$ if needed gives constants $v_0,L,T_0>0$ such that $V(P,W)\ge v_0$, $|\sqrt{V(P,W)}-\sqrt{V(P',W)}|\le L\|P-P'\|_2$ on $U$, and $T(P,W)\le T_0$ there. The derivative bounds follow from [F11] and compactness of the finite-dimensional neighborhood.

There is also a global constant $B<\infty$ with $V(P,W)\le B$ for every input law. Indeed, let $w_0$ be the least positive transition probability of $W$. If $P(x)>0$ and $W(y\mid x)>0$, then $(PW)(y)\ge P(x)W(y\mid x)$, so $|\imath_P(x;y)|\le |\ln w_0|+|\ln P(x)|$. The function $t(1+|\ln t|)^2$ extends continuously to zero and is bounded on $[0,1]$; summing the resulting finite bound over $x$ gives $\mathbb E\imath_P^2\le B$ and hence $V(P,W)\le B$.

Fix a code whose every codeword has type $P$ and let $Q_n=(PW)^n$. For message $m$ with codeword $x_m^n$, put $L_m(y^n)=\ln[W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)/Q_n(y^n)]$ on its charged support. Every codeword of type $P$ gives the same distribution of $L_m$ under its channel law, with mean $nI(P,W)$ and variance $nV(P,W)$; the summands are independent and row counts are $nP(x)$. For any $\gamma>0$, split each decoder region at $t=\ln M-\gamma$. On $L_m\le t$, $W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)\le Me^{-\gamma}Q_n(y^n)$. Averaging over messages and using disjoint decoder regions gives $1-e_{\rm av}\le\Pr\{L>\ln M-\gamma\}+e^{-\gamma},\qquad F_L(\ln M-\gamma)\le e_{\rm av}+e^{-\gamma}.$

For $P\in U$, Berry–Esseen [F7] applied to the centered independent row log-likelihood terms in step 1.4 gives a uniform bound $\sup_z|F_L(nI(P,W)+\sqrt{nV(P,W)}z)-\Phi(z)|\le B_0/\sqrt n,$ where $B_0=1088T_0/v_0^{3/2}$. If $e_{\rm av}\le\epsilon+n^{-1/2}$ and $\gamma=\tfrac12\ln n$, step 1.4 yields $\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln M-\gamma-nI(P,W)}{\sqrt{nV(P,W)}}\right)\le\epsilon+(B_0+2)n^{-1/2}.$ Since $\epsilon$ is fixed in $(0,1)$, choose a compact interval about $z_\epsilon$ on which the positive density $\varphi$ has lower bound $m>0$. The mean-value theorem [F12] gives $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(v)|\ge m|u-v|$ there, so the inverse is locally Lipschitz at $\epsilon$. Hence, uniformly for such types, $\ln M\le nI(P,W)+\sqrt{nV(P,W)}\,z_\epsilon+\tfrac12\ln n+O(1),\qquad z_\epsilon:=\Phi^{-1}(\epsilon).$

Fix $\delta>0$ so that $U$ contains the $\delta$-neighborhood of $\Pi(W)$. On the compact set $\operatorname{dist}(P,\Pi(W))\ge\delta$, continuity and the definition of $\Pi(W)$ give $I(P,W)\le C-\eta$ for some $\eta>0$. If a constant-composition code there had $\ln M-\gamma>nI(P,W)+K\sqrt n$, then on $L>nI(P,W)+K\sqrt n$, the squared centered deviation exceeds $K^2n$, so its indicator is at most $(L-nI(P,W))^2/(K^2n)$. Taking expectations and using step 1.3 gives $F_L(\ln M-\gamma)\ge1-B/K^2$. Choose $K$ with $1-B/K^2>\epsilon$; this contradicts step 1.4 and $e_{\rm av}\le\epsilon+n^{-1/2}$ for large $n$. Therefore $\ln M\le n(C-\eta)+K\sqrt n+\tfrac12\ln n$, which is below the claimed normal upper bound for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $P^*\in\Pi(W)$ attain $V_{\min}$. By [F5], under $P^*W$ the information density has mean $C$ and variance $V_{\min}$; its third absolute centered moment $T^*<\infty$. Apply [F8] to $P^{*n}$. For $\gamma=\tfrac12\ln n$, the DT expectation is at most $\Pr\{S_n\le\ln((M-1)/2)+\gamma\}+e^{-\gamma},$ by splitting at the displayed threshold. Berry–Esseen [F7] bounds this by $\Phi((t-nC)/\sqrt{nV_{\min}})+1088T^*/(V_{\min}^{3/2}\sqrt n)+n^{-1/2}$, where $t=\ln((M-1)/2)+\gamma$.

Put $a=-z_\epsilon>0$ and $d=\operatorname{dist}_2(P,\Pi(W))$. For $P\in U$, choose a nearest $P_0\in\Pi(W)$, so $V(P_0,W)\ge V_{\min}$. By [F6] and step 1.2, $nI(P,W)-a\sqrt{nV(P,W)}\le nC-a\sqrt{nV_{\min}}-n\alpha d^2+aL\sqrt n\,d\le nC-a\sqrt{nV_{\min}}+\frac{a^2L^2}{4\alpha}.$ Together with step 2.1 this gives the desired $nC+\sqrt{nV_{\min}}z_\epsilon+O(\ln n)$ upper bound for nearby constant-composition codes.

Set $u_n=\epsilon-(1088T^*/V_{\min}^{3/2}+2)n^{-1/2}$ and $t_n=nC+\sqrt{nV_{\min}}\Phi^{-1}(u_n)$, for large $n$ with $u_n>0$. We have $C>0$: if $C=0$, every point-mass input is a CAID and has zero dispersion, contradicting $V_{\min}>0$. Choose $M=1+\lfloor2e^{t_n-\gamma}\rfloor$, which is at least two for large $n$ and satisfies $t\le t_n$ and $\ln M\ge t_n-\gamma-O(1)$. Step 2.3 and [F7] give a deterministic code with average error at most $\epsilon-n^{-1/2}$ and $\ln M\ge nC+\sqrt{nV_{\min}}z_\epsilon-O(\ln n),$ using local Lipschitz continuity of $\Phi^{-1}$ at $\epsilon$ from [F12].

For an arbitrary code of size $M$ with individual errors $e_m\ge0$ and average error at most $\epsilon$, put $\tau=\epsilon+n^{-1/2}$ and let $b$ count the messages with $e_m>\tau$. If $b>0$, then $b\tau<\sum_{e_m>\tau}e_m\le\sum_m e_m\le M\epsilon$, so the retained count $g=M-b$ satisfies $g>M(1-\epsilon/\tau)=M/(1+\epsilon\sqrt n)$. If $b=0$, then $g=M$ satisfies the same weak lower bound. Hence in all cases $g\ge\lceil M/(1+\epsilon\sqrt n)\rceil\ge1$, and every retained message has error at most $\tau$. Restrict the decoder to the retained set, mapping removed outputs to a fixed retained label; no retained message's error increases. Among at most $K=(n+1)^{|\mathcal X|}$ input types, one type subcode has at least $\lceil g/K\rceil$ messages, hence at least $M/[(1+\epsilon\sqrt n)K]$. Its logarithmic size loss is therefore at most $\ln(1+\epsilon\sqrt n)+|\mathcal X|\ln(n+1)=O(\ln n)$ and its average error is at most $\epsilon+n^{-1/2}$. Applying steps 2.1, 2.2, and 3.1 to this type subcode gives $\ln M\le nC+\sqrt{nV_{\min}}z_\epsilon+O(\ln n).$

A code with maximal error at most $\epsilon$ also has average error at most $\epsilon$, so step 4.1 bounds maximal-error code sizes as well. The largest code sizes are finite: average success is at most $|\mathcal Y|^n/M$, since each output is decoded as only one message and contributes at most one to the sum of message success probabilities. Thus $M\le |\mathcal Y|^n/(1-\epsilon)$ for either criterion.

For all sufficiently large $n$ with $n^{-1/2}<\epsilon$, let $M$ be the size of the code of step 3.2 and let $b$ count its messages with individual error $e_m>\epsilon$. If $b>0$, then $b\epsilon<\sum_{e_m>\epsilon}e_m\le\sum_m e_m\le M(\epsilon-n^{-1/2})$, so its retained count $g=M-b$ satisfies $g>M/(\epsilon\sqrt n)$. If $b=0$, $g=M\ge M/(\epsilon\sqrt n)$ because $\epsilon\sqrt n>1$. Therefore $g\ge\lceil M/(\epsilon\sqrt n)\rceil\ge1$, and every retained message has error at most $\epsilon$. Restricting the decoder as in step 4.1 does not increase those errors. The resulting code has maximal error at most $\epsilon$ and log size at least $\ln M-\ln(\epsilon\sqrt n)$, so it loses at most $\tfrac12\ln n+\ln\epsilon=\tfrac12\ln n+O(1)$. Combining the average achievability from step 3.2 and the maximal construction above with the average and maximal converses from steps 4.1 and 5.1 proves both equalities in the Statement.

Let $P,Q$ be probability vectors on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$
([[def-finite-probability-vector]]). They define finite probability spaces
with outcome weights $p_x$ and $q_x$, respectively
([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). For $h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, write
$E_Ph:=\sum_xp_xh(x)$ and $E_Qh:=\sum_xq_xh(x)$; these are the finite
expectations ([[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]]). Test the
simple null $H_0:P$ against the simple alternative $H_1:Q$. A randomized test is a function
$\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $\phi(x)$ is the probability of rejecting
$H_0$ after observing $x$; thus $1-\phi(x)$ is the probability of accepting
$H_0$ ([[def-randomized-test]]). Its type-I error is
$\sum_xp_x\phi(x)$, and its type-II error is
$\sum_xq_x(1-\phi(x))$ ([[def-test-size-and-power]]).

For $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, define the oriented type-II testing function
$$\beta_\epsilon(P,Q):=\inf_{\substack{\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]\\\sum_xp_x\phi(x)\le\epsilon}}\sum_xq_x(1-\phi(x)).$$
Here the first argument is the null law and the second is the alternative
law; $\epsilon$ bounds rejection under the first law, while the objective is
acceptance of the null under the second. The feasible set is nonempty because
$\phi=0$ is allowed, and every objective value lies in $[0,1]$. Thus the set
of objective values is nonempty and bounded below in $\mathbb R$, so it has a
real infimum: [[def-real-numbers]] identifies $\mathbb R$ with the
Cauchy-sequence reals, [[thm-reals-ordered-field]] gives their ordered-field
structure, and [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] gives their
least-upper-bound property. [[def-complete-ordered-field]] gives the
equivalent infimum property. Since the set also lies in $[0,1]$, that
infimum lies in $[0,1]$. In the
Neyman–Pearson-region convention that constrains null acceptance below by
$\gamma$, this is the lower boundary value at $\gamma=1-\epsilon$.

Let a finite-DMC code have $M\ge1$ messages and average error $\epsilon$. For any output probability vector $Q_{Y^n}$, let $P_{MY^n}(m,y^n)=M^{-1}W^n(y^n\mid x_m^n)$ be the true joint law and let $\widetilde Q_{MY^n}(m,y^n)=M^{-1}Q_{Y^n}(y^n)$. With the type-II testing function $\beta_\epsilon$ of [[def-finite-hypothesis-testing-beta]], which constrains rejection under its first argument, one has
$$\beta_\epsilon(P_{MY^n},\widetilde Q_{MY^n})\le\frac1M.$$

At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is

Write $\psi=1-\phi$ for the acceptance probability. The constraint in [F1] is $\mathbb E_P\psi\ge1-p$, and the objective is $\mathbb E_{\widetilde Q}\psi$. Let $s$ be the sum of $\psi$ on the two correct pairs and $t$ its sum on the two crossover pairs. Then $0\le s,t\le2$, the constraint is $(1-p)s/2+pt/2\ge1-p$, and the objective is $(s+t)/4$.

If $s\ge2$, the objective is at least $1/2$. If $s<2$, the constraint forces $t\ge(1-p)(2-s)/p$, so $s+t\ge s+\frac{1-p}{p}(2-s)\ge2,$ where the last inequality follows from $(1-p)/p>1$ and $s<2$. Thus every randomized feasible test has objective at least $1/2$. Taking $\psi=1$ on the two correct pairs and $0$ on the crossover pairs attains constraint equality and objective $1/2$. Hence $\beta_p=1/2=1/M$, as also bounded by [F2].
